questions.question: Relational databases store data primarily as:
options: Only opaque blobs with no query language at all.
Tables and rows, with SQL joins across tables.
Only ring positions on a consistent-hashing circle.
Only DNS TXT records replicated to every resolver.
questions.explanation: Relational databases represent and store data in tables and rows. You can perform join operations using SQL

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Relational databases represent and store data in tables and rows. You can perform join operations using SQL

questions.question: NoSQL stores are commonly grouped into categories such as:
options: Only “fast” and “slow” with no other distinctions.
Key-value, document, column, and graph stores.
Only Oracle and DB2 under different marketing names.
Only in-memory caches that never persist to disk.
questions.explanation: key-value stores, graph stores, column stores, and document stores

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: key-value stores, graph stores, column stores, and document stores

questions.question: Joins in non-relational databases are:
options: Always richer and faster than SQL joins in every product.
Generally not supported the way SQL databases support them.
Required on every single read path by definition in real production systems at scale.
Performed automatically by the DNS layer for free in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: Join operations are generally not supported in non-relational databases

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: Join operations are generally not supported in non-relational databases

questions.question: DDIA’s building-block view says databases exist to:
options: Render CSS animations for marketing pages only in real production systems at scale.
Store data so the app (or another app) can find it again later.
Replace all caches, queues, and search indexes permanently.
Guarantee zero operational cost at infinite scale in real production systems at scale.
questions.explanation: Store data so that they, or another application, can find it again later (databases)

reference.excerpt: Store data so that they, or another application, can find it again later (databases)

questions.question: True or false: Xu’s default advice is still “start with relational” unless your use case clearly does not fit.
questions.explanation: For most developers, relational databases are the best option

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
reference.excerpt: For most developers, relational databases are the best option

questions.question: Replication is introduced when:
options: You want a single disk with no copies for maximum simplicity under load.
Read load or availability needs exceed what one primary alone should handle.
You delete indexes so every query becomes a full table scan in real production systems at scale.
You ban backups because replicas already mean infinite durability in real production systems at scale.

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
